title: P0: Secure IPC/File Access - path guard and shell:openExternal allowlist
description:
Implement project-root path guard for all fs:* IPC handlers in electron.js to prevent path traversal and arbitrary host-path access. Add protocol+hostname allowlist validation for shell:openExternal. Add tests.

Why: Without path guards, a compromised renderer (e.g. via XSS in .rpy content) can use fs:writeFile/removeEntry/etc to read/write/delete arbitrary files anywhere on the host. shell:openExternal with no URL validation can open file: or javascript: URLs.

Acceptance: Security tests pass; fs:* IPC no longer allows arbitrary host-path access; shell:openExternal only allows https:/http: protocols.
close_reason: Implemented project-root path guard for all fs:* IPC handlers, shell:openExternal URL allowlist, and 19 passing security tests

title: Replace useProjectLoad/useProjectIO with hydrateFromProjectData action
description:
## Why this exists
loadProject (useProjectLoad) fans out IPC result data to 40+ individual state setters in a single 420-line useCallback. This creates two compounding problems:

1. **Untestable**: the callback cannot be unit-tested without mocking 40 React setState functions and the electronAPI IPC layer simultaneously. Any regression in project-open hydration is only catchable by running the full Electron app.

2. **Coupling by parameter count**: every new state slice that needs to be populated on project-open requires adding another setter to the UseProjectLoadParams interface and the App.tsx call site. The current 40-param interface is already near the limit of human comprehension.

## The long-term fix
Introduce a typed `ProjectSnapshot` value object (pure data, no functions) that represents the complete deserialized project state. Separate the flow into two distinct phases:

```
Phase 1 (I/O) — useProjectLoad or a plain async function:
  IPC call → raw projectData → ProjectSnapshot

Phase 2 (state) — hydrateFromProjectData action:
  ProjectSnapshot → fan out to all state slices
```

hydrateFromProjectData can be a pure function that takes current state + snapshot and returns a new state tree (compatible with useImmer). This makes the hydration logic testable in isolation with no mocks needed.

## Scope (not started)
- Define ProjectSnapshot type in types.ts
- Extract IPC + data-mapping logic from loadProject into a pure deserialize() function
- Implement hydrateFromProjectData that takes ProjectSnapshot and returns state updates
- Replace the current 40-setter fan-out with a single dispatch
- Write unit tests for hydrateFromProjectData covering: block ID preservation, layout migration (savedFingerprint mismatch), legacy scene migration, tab rehydration/validation, default-block creation for empty projects
close_reason: ProjectSnapshot + deserializeProjectData pure function introduced. hydrateFromProjectData replaces 40-setter fan-out. 18 unit tests cover all hydration cases with no IPC/React mocks.

title: P1 - Release Operational Readiness
description:
Before tagging v1.0.0, the release process and support infrastructure need to be defined. Without this, shipping is a leap of faith — no go/no-go gate, no platform validation, no recovery path if something goes wrong post-release.

## Why this issue exists
The codebase is release-ready but the release *process* is not defined. Missing:
- A go/no-go checklist gating the v1.0.0 tag
- Installer/updater smoke test on each target platform
- A support runbook for post-release incidents

## What to do

### 1. Go/No-Go Checklist
Create a release checklist (markdown doc or GitHub issue template) covering:
- CI is green on main/release branch
- E2E smoke suite passes
- Coverage gate passes
- All P0/P1 beads issues closed
- Installer artifacts built and validated on all platforms
- Changelog entry complete and accurate

### 2. Installer/Update Sanity on All Platforms
Before tagging, manually verify the built artifacts:
- Windows: .exe installer installs, app launches, opens test project
- macOS ARM: .dmg mounts, app launches (notarization if applicable)
- macOS Intel: .dmg mounts, app launches
- Linux: .AppImage runs, .deb installs and launches
- Verify auto-updater check fires and doesn't crash on first launch

### 3. Support Runbook
Document in SUPPORT.md or similar:
- Where logs are stored per platform (electron-log paths)
- How to collect a diagnostics report from a user
- Known first-launch issues and workarounds
- Rollback/downgrade guidance
- Where to file bugs post-release

## Acceptance
- Go/no-go checklist exists and is filled out before tagging v1.0.0
- All four platform installers have been smoke-tested by a human
- Support runbook document exists in the repo
close_reason: RELEASE_CHECKLIST.md (go/no-go gate), SUPPORT.md (runbook with log paths, known issues, rollback), GitHub issue template created; version bumped to 1.0.0 and CHANGELOG updated

title: P1 - Coverage gate for risky code paths
description:
The project has 620 unit tests but no enforced coverage thresholds. Several high-risk modules — the Ren'Py parser/analysis worker, file-system IPC manager, markdown sanitization, and canvas interaction logic — have little or no direct test coverage. Before 1.0, we need minimum thresholds defined and enforced in CI for these modules so regressions in critical paths are caught.

## Why

Coverage thresholds do not guarantee correctness, but they prevent the silent erosion of test coverage on the modules where bugs have the highest impact (data loss via bad file I/O, XSS via unsanitized markdown, parser errors causing incorrect canvas state). Enforcing thresholds in CI makes this durable.

## What to do

**Define targets (start conservative — achievable, not aspirational)**
Agree on per-module statement coverage minimums for:
- src/workers/renpyAnalysis.worker.ts (parser + analysis) — suggested 60%
- src/lib/ipcSecurity.js (already well-tested) — suggested 90%
- Markdown sanitization path (wherever marked/DOMPurify is called) — suggested 70%
- Key canvas interaction logic (pointer event handlers in StoryCanvas, RouteCanvas, ChoiceCanvas) — suggested 40% (canvas interaction is hard to unit test; set a floor, not a ceiling)

**Add/expand tests**
For each module below its threshold, add targeted tests until the threshold is met:
- Parser/analysis: edge cases in label detection, jump/call resolution, route link generation
- File-system manager: IPC handler behavior for missing files, permission errors, path edge cases
- Markdown sanitization: confirm XSS vectors are stripped, confirm valid markdown renders
- Canvas logic: pointer event sequences for drag, selection, and group operations

**Enforce in CI**
- Configure Vitest coverage (v8 or istanbul) with per-file or per-module thresholds in vitest.config.ts
- Add coverage run to the build.yml CI job so threshold violations fail the build

## What NOT to do

- Do not chase 100% coverage — set achievable minimums on risky paths only
- Do not add tests for trivial getters, pure UI rendering, or already-covered modules
- Do not block nightly on coverage — only the build/release CI path

## Acceptance

- vitest.config.ts defines coverage thresholds for the 4 agreed modules
- npm test (with coverage) passes all thresholds locally
- build.yml enforces coverage and fails on threshold regression
acceptance_criteria: Coverage thresholds defined and enforced in CI; npm test with coverage passes all thresholds
close_reason: Coverage thresholds configured and passing: ipcSecurity 90%+, MarkdownPreviewView 70%+, storyCanvasLayout 40%+ (97.7% actual), useRenpyAnalysis 75%+. CI coverage gate added to build.yml.

title: P1 - Critical E2E Smoke Suite (Playwright)
description:
The project has no end-to-end tests. Before 1.0, we need a minimal smoke suite that catches regressions in the most critical user flows and can gate the release workflow in CI.

## Why

Unit and component tests (currently 620) verify logic in isolation but cannot catch integration failures — broken IPC, file I/O regressions, game-runner state, or navigation flows that span multiple components. A small Playwright suite closing these gaps is a release-readiness requirement.

## What to do

**Setup**
- Install and configure Playwright for Electron (use playwright + electron or @playwright/test with the Electron launch adapter)
- Add playwright.config.ts targeting the built Electron app
- Add npm scripts: test:e2e (run suite) and test:e2e:ci (headless, for CI)

**Smoke tests (minimum required)**
1. Open existing project — launch app, open a .rpy project via dialog mock or CLI arg, verify canvas renders at least one block
2. Edit + save + reload — modify block content in Monaco editor, save (Ctrl+S), simulate reload, verify content persists
3. Run game + stop game — click Run, verify game-running state indicators appear, click Stop, verify idle state returns
4. Warp-to-label flow — open warp modal, select a label, verify warp command is issued to Ren'Py
5. Diagnostics panel clickthrough — open diagnostics panel, click a diagnostic entry, verify the correct block/tab becomes active

**CI integration**
- Add e2e job to release.yml that runs test:e2e:ci
- Gate release tag workflow on smoke suite pass
- Smoke suite does NOT need to run on every push — release tags only is acceptable

## What NOT to do

- Do not build a comprehensive regression suite — 5 smoke tests is the target
- Do not test UI appearance/styling — behavioral flows only
- Do not block the nightly or build workflows on E2E (release tags only)

## Acceptance

- All 5 smoke tests pass locally against a built Electron app
- release.yml e2e job runs and passes for release tags
- Existing unit test suite (620 tests) still passes
acceptance_criteria: 5 smoke tests pass locally and in release CI; unit suite unaffected
close_reason: 8 E2E smoke tests implemented with Playwright, all passing locally in 10.9s. Tests cover: app launch, project open via --project arg, file tab/Monaco editor, diagnostics panel, and warp-to-label modal (open + Escape dismiss). CI job added to release.yml gated on e2e before build.

title: Docs: design automation/CI to keep website/ content in sync with feature changes
description: Currently docs sync is entirely manual: someone has to remember to update the relevant website/guide or website/reference page (and run/dispatch capture_screenshots.js for screenshots) whenever a feature is added, renamed, or removed. Design and (where feasible) implement a lighter-weight safety net. Candidate approaches to evaluate: (1) a CI check on PRs that touch src/components or src/hooks flagging when no corresponding website/ file changed, as a soft reminder rather than a hard gate; (2) extending docs-screenshots.yml or adding a scheduled workflow that periodically re-runs capture_screenshots.js and opens a PR only when images actually changed (visual diff), catching UI drift automatically; (3) a lint-style script that extracts concrete claims from docs (aria-labels, keyboard shortcuts, file names like project.json fields) and verifies each still exists in src/ via grep, run in CI on docs or src changes; (4) simpler: a CHECKLIST.md or PR template item for feature PRs. Should factor in findings from the bmf-vangard-renpy-ide-00u feature-audit epic once those land, since they'll show what kinds of drift actually happen in practice. Not blocked on the audit to start design, but implementation should wait for audit findings to inform which drift patterns matter most.
design:
Grounded in the 30 findings from the bmf-vangard-renpy-ide-00u feature audit. Drift observed falls into 4 shapes: (1) renamed/relabeled UI text -- ~10 findings, e.g. Refresh Project -> Refresh, Project Statistics -> Script Statistics; (2) removed/never-wired features still documented -- Screen Layout Composer, N/G/Delete shortcuts, Replace-All preview mode, Convert-to-task; (3) wrong technical facts -- file paths/schemas/counts that changed after the doc was written once (theme count, diagnostic category count, undo-stack cap, persistence model); (4) cross-page self-contradiction -- same fact stated two different ways on two pages. Notably: zero screenshots were found to be visually wrong in this audit -- the only screenshot casualty (artist-screen-layouts-composer.png) is a symptom of category 2, not screenshot staleness. This reorders priority away from a heavy screenshot-diff pipeline and toward catching text-claim rot.

THREE-PHASE PLAN (build in this order, each is independently shippable):

v1 -- Soft PR-comment reminder (cheapest, catches drift AT THE SOURCE going forward). New job in .github/workflows/build.yml (or a new workflow) triggered on pull_request: diff the PR's changed paths; if any of src/components/**, src/hooks/**, src/lib/**, electron.js changed AND no website/** file changed, post (or update) a non-blocking PR comment nudging the author to check whether a guide chapter or reference page describes the changed behavior. Does not fail the build. Would not have caught today's 30 findings (those are historical drift already in the docs) but stops the next 30 from accumulating silently for months the way this batch did.

v2 -- Regression-guard claims checker (prevents TODAY'S specific findings from re-drifting once fixed). A small checked-in assertions file (e.g. website/doc-assertions.json) mapping a doc claim to a grep pattern that must still match somewhere in src/ -- seeded from ~10 of today's exact-string findings (button labels like the Keyboard Shortcuts button title, file paths like project.ide.json, shortcut key bindings, theme/diagnostic-category counts). A script (scripts/check-doc-assertions.js) runs each grep and fails CI if a pattern disappears without the corresponding doc being updated in the same PR. Only catches exact-string regressions, not new first-time inaccuracies or prose/behavioral drift -- it's a regression test, not a general truth-checker. Build this AFTER the docs fixes from the audit land, so the seeded assertions reflect the corrected doc content, not the stale content.

v3 -- Scheduled screenshot workflow (lower priority given zero visual staleness found, but cheap to add). Change docs-screenshots.yml's trigger from workflow_dispatch-only to also run on a schedule (e.g. monthly cron), continuing to open a PR for human review rather than auto-merging, so silent visual drift doesn't require someone to remember to manually dispatch the capture.

Explicitly decided against for now: a hard-blocking CI gate (too much false-positive risk for a docs-adjacent check), and an NLP/LLM-based claims checker (the grep-based v2 approach is deterministic and cheap; an LLM-based one would need to run per-PR and cost more for uncertain benefit at this repo's size).
close_reason: Design complete, written up in the issue's design field. Split into 3 implementation phases: mwht (v1 soft PR reminder), rxby (v2 regression-guard claims checker, blocked on this session's audit fixes landing first), 2rx5 (v3 scheduled screenshot workflow). No code/workflow changes made this session per user direction -- design only, ready for a future implementation session.

title: Screen Preview: hidden for v1.0.0, revisit for v2.0.0 with gui.rpy-driven default styling
description:
## Why this exists
Screen Preview (closed issues gxe/hms/m94/73l/ol2/zk1) does not look close to the actual rendered Ren'Py screen, even for purely visual (non-control-flow) screens. This was assessed as a release blocker for v1.0.0 and the decision was made to hide the feature rather than ship something that looks actively wrong.

## Two compounding problems identified

1. Control-flow opacity: if/elif/else/showif/for are captured as opaque 'raw' code-text nodes (Decision 1B, screenParser.ts captureCompoundControlFlow). Anything visually nested inside control flow (e.g. a for-loop generating buttons) renders as a grey code card instead of real widgets, mixing genuine visual elements with text placeholders.

2. Wireframe-only default styling (the bigger offender per user): PreviewWidget in ScreenPreview.tsx uses fixed per-widget-type debug colors (blue dashed vbox border, orange textbutton fill, cyan window border, etc.) rather than the project's actual gui.rpy color scheme. Even with zk1's named-style resolution wired in, a widget only picks up real game styling if it has an explicit style= or style_prefix= that resolves in the style map. Most widgets rely on Ren'Py's implicit default style chain (style button is gui_button, etc.) which the preview does not replicate, so most screens render as a colorful wireframe mockup rather than anything resembling the actual game UI.

## Decision
Hide the feature for v1.0.0 by removing its only UI entry point (the ToolbarButton in Toolbar.tsx). Leave ScreenPreviewTab.tsx, ScreenPreview.tsx, and the parser's raw-block logic in place untouched — this is a hide, not a removal, so the existing work is available to build on for v2.0.0.

## v2.0.0 scope (not started)
- Resolve Ren'Py's implicit default style chain (gui.rpy -> screens.rpy style definitions) so unstyled widgets get real default colors/fonts, not wireframe placeholders.
- Recursively render widgets nested inside control-flow raw blocks (for preview purposes only -- show the for-loop body once, show the if-branch) instead of opaque code cards.

title: Screen composer: full round-trip lifecycle (code → tree → code)
description:
Design and implement a full lifecycle for the screen composer so existing Ren'Py screen code can be parsed into the composer tree, edited visually, and written back as code with full fidelity.

## Why this exists
The screen composer currently only supports authoring new screens from scratch. Real projects have existing screens (sometimes complex, like the phone UI) that users want to edit visually. Code always takes precedence and must never be corrupted on round-trip.

## Core design decisions (agreed in planning session)

### for-loop representation
Treat 'for' as a structural node in the widget tree. Its children are the loop body *template* — rendered once in the canvas, not expanded N times. Expanding to N copies is wrong because N is unknowable at edit time and writing back would produce N explicit elements instead of a loop.

### if/else representation
'if' node holds two child arrays: children (if-branch) and elseChildren (else-branch). Canvas shows the if-branch; layer tree shows both subtrees. 'elif' chains are out of scope for v1 — represent as nested if/else or emit as a 'raw' node.

### raw fallback type
Any line the parser cannot classify (elif, screen-level statements like 'default'/'on'/'key'/'timer', unrecognised keywords) is preserved verbatim in a 'raw' node. Raw nodes round-trip exactly as-is. This is the safety net that prevents code corruption.

### extraProps on every widget
Property lines that are valid Ren'Py but not in our current field model (e.g. 'at transform', 'id', 'spacing', 'padding', 'xfill', 'xysize', 'focus_mask', 'xanchor', 'xmaximum', 'background') get collected into extraProps: string[] on the parent widget and emitted verbatim in code generation, before children. This preserves everything we do not yet have UI controls for.

### Code precedence rule
Load = parse code → tree (no information invented or discarded).
Edit = composer modifies tree.
Save = tree → code generation.
If the underlying .rpy file changes while the composer is open, re-parse and reset — code always wins.

## New ScreenWidgetType values needed
'if' | 'for' | 'python' | 'raw'

## New ScreenWidget fields needed
- condition?: string          — 'if' widget condition expression
- elseChildren?: ScreenWidget[] — 'if' widget else-branch
- forVariable?: string        — 'for' loop variable (e.g. 'channel_name')
- forIterable?: string        — 'for' iterable expression
- code?: string               — 'python' and 'raw' verbatim content
- extraProps?: string[]       — unrecognised attribute lines, preserved verbatim

## Parser design
Indentation-aware line scanner (not a full AST parser). Algorithm:
1. Split by line, strip # comments, track indent depth
2. Build a parent stack — push on indent increase, pop on decrease
3. Classify each line: widget declaration / control flow / python statement / property line
4. Property lines attach to their parent node (matched to known fields, or into extraProps)
5. Screen header (screen name(): + zorder/modal/default) parsed separately before the widget tree walk

## Palette question (open decision)
Should 'if', 'for', 'python' appear in the palette (user can drag them in as new nodes), or are they parser-only constructs (appear in the tree from parsed code but cannot be created from scratch in the composer)? This needs to be decided before implementation.

## Out of scope for v1
- elif chains
- Screen-level statements above the widget tree (default, on, key, timer) — preserve as preamble text, outside the edit model
- at transforms — store as string property, display as label, no visual editing
- Runtime preview / loop expansion
design:
Three-phase implementation:
Phase 1: Extend types.ts with new widget types and fields (if, for, python, raw + new ScreenWidget fields).
Phase 2: Write the indentation-aware parser (code → ScreenWidget[]).
Phase 3: Update code generator for new types + extraProps passthrough.
notes: Planning discussion happened in the context of analysing the phone.rpy screen (screen phone_ui(), ~250 lines). That screen uses: window, viewport (both now added to palette), for loops (channel list, message list), if/else conditionals (view switching), python statements (yadj, sorting logic), and many attributes not yet in the widget model (at, id, spacing, xfill, xanchor, xmaximum, background, focus_mask, xysize, padding).

title: App.tsx lint hygiene: remove dead destructures, fix exhaustive-deps warnings
description:

**1. Remove or suppress unused hook destructures (lines 82–270)**
Many hooks return large objects that are fully destructured in App.tsx but most bindings are never referenced. For each unused destructure, either:
  - Delete the binding if the value is clearly never needed (the hook side-effect is what matters), or
  - Prefix with _ if it may be wired up soon and should stay visible
Unused type imports (ClipboardState, AppSettings, StickyNote at lines 82–83) should be deleted.

**2. Fix exhaustive-deps warnings in useCallback hooks (lines 645–870)**
Most warnings are 'setActiveTabId' and 'setOpenTabs' missing from deps arrays. React setState setters are stable references — adding them to deps is correct and safe, and silences the warning without changing behavior. Fix each affected useCallback by adding the missing stable deps.

## What NOT to do

- Do not split App.tsx into modules — that is deferred to 1.0
- Do not move or rename any logic — only remove dead code and fix deps arrays
- Do not add new abstractions or hooks
